submission.title: The Death Algorithm
submission.full_story:
The algorithm was supposed to predict quarterly sales, not the exact date Maya would die.

She stared at her laptop screen in DataFlow's empty office, the vending machine humming in the corner like a mechanical heartbeat. The prototype had been running for six hours when it suddenly displayed: "SUBJECT: Maya Chen. TERMINATION: March 15, 2089."

Sixty-five more years. She should feel relieved.

"Jake, you need to see this." Her voice barely a whisper.

Jake stumbled over from his desk, energy drink trembling in his hand. Their startup was hemorrhaging money—three weeks from bankruptcy. This algorithm was supposed to save them.

Maya turned the screen toward him. "It's not predicting sales."

Jake's face went slack. "That's a death date."

"Test yourself."

His fingers fumbled across the keyboard. The screen flickered: "SUBJECT: Jake Morrison. TERMINATION: August 3, 2024."

Six months.

Jake's energy drink hit the floor, fizzing across worn carpet. "No. No, this is just broken code—"

"I've verified it twelve times. The math is perfect."

Maya watched her best friend crumble. His mother's cancer treatments. His daughter's college dreams. All of it ending in six months.

"We could warn people," Maya whispered. "Help them prepare—"

"Or sell it," Jake said, desperation creeping in. "Think what people would pay—"

Maya's phone buzzed. Unknown number.

"We know about the death predictor," a cold voice said. "Ten million. Tonight. Or others will take it from you."

The line went dead.

Maya looked at Jake, whose eyes now held the hollow stare of a man counting down his final days.

They weren't alone anymore.

submission.title: The Death Algorithm
submission.full_story:
Jake hadn't slept in three days, and Maya could see death creeping into his eyes.

He sat at his desk, staring at the screen that had sentenced him: August 3rd, 2024. One hundred and eighty-three days. Maya watched her best friend disappearing in real-time, hollowed out by certainty.

"Emma starts college in September," Jake whispered. "I'll miss move-in day by a month."

Maya's throat constricted. Jake's daughter was his entire world—the reason he'd sacrificed his six-figure corporate salary for their startup gamble. Now their algorithm had transformed that sacrifice into cruel mathematics.

"The ten million," Jake said, voice distant. "It could pay for Emma's education. Mom's cancer treatments. Everything."

"Jake, we don't know who these people are. What they'll do with it."

"Does it matter?" He looked up, and Maya saw something that terrified her: acceptance. "I'm dying anyway. At least this way, it helps someone."

Maya's chest burned. She'd built this algorithm too, but she got sixty-five more years. Jake got six months. The unfairness felt like swallowing glass.

Her phone buzzed: "Parking garage. Sublevel 2. One hour. Come alone."

She showed Jake the message. He stood slowly, movements deliberate.

"You know what's funny about having an expiration date?" Jake said, reaching for his jacket. "Nothing else seems scary anymore."

Maya watched him head toward the door—toward whatever waited in that garage. The algorithm had given them godlike knowledge, and it was destroying them from the inside.

"Jake, wait—"

He paused, hand on the doorknob.

"I can't watch you die twice," Maya said.

But Jake was already walking into the hallway, leaving her alone with the weight of their terrible creation.

submission.title: The Death Algorithm
submission.full_story:
Maya realized the algorithm had been wrong about one thing—it couldn't predict what love would make someone do.

She found Jake in the parking garage, briefcase open beside him, ten million in cash scattered like fallen leaves. The buyers had vanished, leaving only money and the weight of their bargain.

"They took the algorithm," Jake said, voice hollow. "It's over."

Maya knelt beside him, studying his face—gaunt, resigned, already half-ghost. In six months, Emma would be fatherless. His mother would die alone.

"No," Maya said quietly. "It's not."

She pulled out her phone and dialed the number from the mysterious calls.

"We had a deal," the cold voice answered.

"New deal," Maya said. "You want the algorithm's creator? The real architect behind the code? It wasn't Jake."

Jake grabbed her arm. "Maya, what are you doing?"

She met his eyes, seeing past the fear to the father underneath. "I built the death predictor. Jake just helped with implementation. You want the source code that's still in my head? You want the person who can recreate it? Take me instead."

"Maya, no—"

"Forty-eight hours," she continued into the phone. "Let Jake walk away with the money, and I'll give you everything. But if anything happens to him or his family..."

"Accepted," the voice said. "Tomorrow night."

She hung up, watching Jake's face crumble.

"You have sixty-five years," he whispered.

"And you have a daughter who needs her father." Maya's voice broke. "Emma deserves to see you at graduation. Your mom deserves to beat cancer with you there."

Jake pulled her into his arms, both of them shaking.

"I can't let you—"

"It's already done." Maya stepped back, deleting the algorithm from her laptop permanently. "Take the money. Live the life I can't."

In the distance, footsteps echoed. Their time was up.

But Maya felt something unexpected: peace. She'd finally found an equation that mattered more than data.

submission.title: The Death Algorithm: Legacy
submission.full_story:
Emma Morrison had cleaned out her father's office three times, but she kept missing things.

This time it was a laptop hidden behind old tax files, password-protected with her birthday. Dad had died six months ago—lung cancer, three years past his "expiration date"—and Emma was still finding pieces of the man she thought she knew.

The desktop had one folder: "For Emma - When You're Ready."

Inside, a video file and something called "Maya's Algorithm."

Emma clicked the video. Her father's gaunt face filled the screen, recorded during his final weeks.

"Emma, if you're watching this, I'm gone, and you're probably wondering about your benefactor. Maya Chen wasn't just my business partner. She was my best friend, and she saved my life."

Emma's chest tightened. Maya Chen—the mysterious woman who'd funded her MIT education, her mother's medical bills, everything. Dad had always deflected questions about her.

"Maya created something that predicted death dates. Mine was August 3rd, 2024. Hers was March 15, 2089. She traded places with me so I could watch you graduate, walk you down the aisle, be the father you deserved."

The video ended. Emma stared at the second file.

The algorithm was elegant, beautiful code that turned mortality into mathematics. Emma ran it on herself: sixty-eight years remaining.

Then, hands shaking, she typed: "David Park."

Her fiancé. The man she'd marry in two months.

"TERMINATION: November 22, 2025."

One year.

Emma's phone buzzed. David: "Dinner tonight? I have a surprise."

The engagement ring. She'd seen him hiding the jewelry store receipt.

Emma stared at the screen, understanding her father's final gift. He'd lived with this knowledge for years—watching her fall in love with a dying man, knowing she'd face the same choice Maya had made.

Delete the algorithm and let love bloom in ignorance?

Or carry the terrible weight of knowing exactly how much time they had left?

The cursor blinked, waiting.
submission.short_summary: Years after Jake Morrison's death, his daughter Emma discovers the truth about Maya Chen—the woman who secretly funded her education wasn't just her father's business partner, but the creator of a death-prediction algorithm who sacrificed her own life to save Jake's. When Emma finds and runs the algorithm, she discovers her fiancé David has only one year to live. Now she faces the same impossible choice that destroyed the previous generation: delete the algorithm and live in ignorant bliss, or carry the crushing weight of knowing exactly when everyone she loves will die.

submission.title: The Death Algorithm: Bloodline
submission.full_story:
Lily Chen discovered her dead aunt's algorithm was still killing people when she found her own name on the list.

The encrypted files on Nai Nai's laptop contained hundreds of names and dates—all people who'd died exactly when Maya's Death Algorithm predicted. But these weren't natural deaths. They were executions disguised as fate.

"SUBJECT: Lily Chen. TERMINATION: December 15, 2025."

Twelve days.

Her hands trembled as she scrolled through the victims: journalists who'd investigated government corruption, scientists who'd questioned corporate studies, activists who'd threatened powerful interests. The buyers weren't just predicting death—they were scheduling murder, using Maya's creation as the perfect assassination timeline.

A message popped up: "We know you found the files. Delete them, or join the list early."

Lily stared at her grandmother across the kitchen table, peacefully doing crossword puzzles. Nai Nai had spent two years secretly documenting the algorithm's victims, risking everything to honor Maya's memory.

"Why didn't you tell me?" Lily whispered, showing her the screen.

Nai Nai's weathered hands stilled. "Because I knew you'd try to stop me. Just like Maya tried to stop Jake."

"They'll kill us both."

"Maybe. Or maybe we expose them first." Nai Nai's eyes held the same steel that had run in Maya's veins. "Your aunt died believing she was saving one life. She never knew she was creating a weapon."

Lily looked at the delete key, then at her grandmother's determined face.

Maya had sacrificed herself for love. Nai Nai was risking everything for justice.

Now Lily had to choose: save herself and let the killing continue, or honor her family's legacy and fight back with twelve days to live.

The cursor blinked, waiting for her decision.

Together with her grandmother, who has been secretly documenting the victims, Lily must decide whether to delete the evidence and save herself, or expose the conspiracy and honor her family's legacy of sacrifice. The intimate family drama maintains the series' focus on personal moral choices while expanding the universe to show the algorithm's broader societal impact.
